input.rationale: Continuing the authorized source work on the deferred transport surface: reading the TCP stream layer, the stream-context lifecycle and the in-process peer registration, and correcting one item I had listed in the previous feedback without having read it. feedback.answered: Three more parts are now sourced. TCP stream layer: newTCPTransport binds with net.Listen("tcp", bindAddr), wraps the listener in TCPStreamLayer with an optional advertise address, rejects a non-TCP listener address (errNotTCP) or an unspecified/absent advertise address (errNotAdvertisable) before creating the transport through a creator callback, and Dial/Accept/Close/Addr are plain net.DialTimeout/listener delegation with Addr preferring the advertised address (tcp_transport.go 23-117). Correction: the TLS configuration item I listed previously was an assumption, not a reading; there is no TLS code in the captured library (no NetworkTransportConfig.TLSConfig and no tls package use outside tests), so TLS can only come from a caller-supplied StreamLayer, and that item is withdrawn rather than left as an unread library responsibility. Stream context: setupStreamContext creates a cancellable context, getStreamContext reads it under its lock, and CloseStreams releases every pooled connection and then cancels and recreates the context under both the pool and context locks, with the code's own comment that the ordering is required so handlers cannot end up holding a never-cancellable context (net_transport.go 285-331); Close closes shutdownCh and the stream layer once (333-345). In-process registration: Connect/Disconnect/DisconnectAll mutate the peers map under the transport lock, and Disconnect additionally closes and compacts any pipelines registered for that peer (inmem_transport.go 215-250).
remaining: The in-process peer consumer-channel capacity was not read, so how many in-process RPCs can queue before a send blocks is still unknown.
Whether an address-provider change can race an in-flight dial was read only at the level of the address lock in getProviderAddressOrFallback.
The heartbeat classification read earlier was not re-checked against exactly what the leader's heartbeat goroutine emits.

StreamLayer implementations supplied by callers remain outside the library; anything a caller wraps around TCPStreamLayer is not a library responsibility, but no library-side TLS or stream-wrapping helper exists to map.

Previously recorded open items are unchanged: installSnapshot watermark reachability from a legal leader history, the compacted-leader variant of the truncation-failure case, and execution corroboration of the two reading-based consequences.

selections.rationale: Recover core understanding of the HashiCorp raft (Go) implementation: describe the formation/advancement line and the authority/term-context line from read source, and explain how the two connect. The map name cites the actual owner/handlers observed in raft.go, commitment.go, fsm.go, replication.go, api.go and snapshot.go; both core paths are grounded and the connection is the term fence on entries plus the startIndex commitment restriction and the ErrLeadershipLost sweep on step-down.

feedback.answered: The initial two-line question is answered for this implementation: decisions form as (index,term) log entries replicated by per-peer goroutines, and advance only when commitment.recalculate finds a quorum voter match at or beyond the leader's term startIndex; authority is a durable per-instance term plus at most one persisted vote, and context is adopted from any higher-term RPC. The connection is the term on every entry, the startIndex commitment restriction on prior-term entries, the ErrLeadershipLost answer to pending futures on step-down, and the rollback of an uncommitted configuration when a follower truncates a conflicting suffix.

after.purpose: Form a decision (leader election / log agreement) and advance the replicated log legally.

formation.explanation: A decision is formed as a log entry and advanced only after a quorum has durably stored it. The leader's dispatchLogs assigns (index, term) to each logFuture, stores it locally and records its own match; each peer's followerReplication goroutine copies entries with AppendEntries and, on success, records that peer's durable match index through commitment.match. commitment.recalculate sorts the voter match indexes, takes the quorum-position match and advances commitIndex only when it is both above the current value and at or beyond the term's startIndex. leaderLoop consumes commitCh, moves the inflight prefix up to the commit index and hands it to the FSM goroutine. A follower mirrors this by clamping its commit index to min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex) and applying the same logs.

context.explanation: Authority is a per-instance, durable term plus at most one vote. A follower that stops hearing from a leader starts a candidate loop that raises currentTerm (persisted first) and solicits votes, optionally behind a non-mutating pre-vote. A vote is granted only to a candidate in the configuration whose log is at least as up to date, and only after the vote is persisted, so the same term cannot vote twice even across restart. Any RPC carrying a higher term forces the receiver to Follower and adopts the sender's term and, for leader RPCs, the sender's leader identity. A leader keeps authority while a quorum of voters is in recent contact and abandons it on a newer term, a failed verification, or a lapsed lease.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the term fence carried by every entry. A log entry is only meaningful together with the term of the leader that wrote it: a follower accepts new entries only when the previous-log coordinate matches its own log and only after adopting a term that is not older, and a new leader may not commit an entry from an earlier term merely because it is stored on a majority — commitment.startIndex forces the current term's opening no-op (or an equivalent entry) to be committed first. Conversely, authority transitions constrain which pending support may still be consumed: when a leader steps down it answers every inflight logFuture and pending verifyFuture with ErrLeadershipLost, and a follower that truncates a conflicting suffix also rolls its latest configuration back to the committed one, so an uncommitted configuration cannot survive on a minority that lost the election.

On the transport side, netPipeline sends the request first and then hands the future to inprogressCh, while a single decodeResponses goroutine takes futures from that channel in order, decodes one response per future on the same connection and publishes completed futures on doneCh (net_transport.go 817-905); the channel is sized maxInFlight-2 so at most maxInFlight requests are outstanding, and Close releases the connection and closes shutdownCh. feedback.answered: Three previously open transport questions are answered by reading. First, a pooled connection is exclusive: getPooledConn takes connPoolLock, pops the last entry of the per-target slice, nils the slot and truncates the slice before returning (net_transport.go 366-378), so one connection cannot be handed to two callers concurrently, and returnConn only re-pools below maxPool (434-446). formation.explanation: A decision is formed as a log entry and advanced only after a quorum has durably stored it. The leader's dispatchLogs assigns (index, term) to each logFuture, stores it locally and records its own match; each peer's followerReplication goroutine copies entries with AppendEntries and, on success, records that peer's durable match index through commitment.match. commitment.recalculate sorts the voter match indexes, takes the quorum-position match and advances commitIndex only when it is both above the current value and at or beyond the term's startIndex. leaderLoop consumes commitCh, moves the inflight prefix up to the commit index and hands it to the FSM goroutine. A follower mirrors this by clamping its commit index to min(LeaderCommitIndex, lastIndex) and applying the same logs.

context.explanation: Authority is a per-instance, durable term plus at most one vote. A follower that stops hearing from a leader starts a candidate loop that raises currentTerm (persisted first) and solicits votes, optionally behind a non-mutating pre-vote. A vote is granted only to a candidate in the configuration whose log is at least as up to date, and only after the vote is persisted, so the same term cannot vote twice even across restart. Any RPC carrying a higher term forces the receiver to Follower and adopts the sender's term and, for leader RPCs, the sender's leader identity. A leader keeps authority while a quorum of voters is in recent contact and abandons it on a newer term, a failed verification, or a lapsed lease.

connection.explanation: The two core lines meet at the term fence carried by every entry. A log entry is only meaningful together with the term of the leader that wrote it: a follower accepts new entries only when the previous-log coordinate matches its own log and only after adopting a term that is not older, and a new leader may not commit an entry from an earlier term merely because it is stored on a majority — commitment.startIndex forces the current term's opening no-op (or an equivalent entry) to be committed first. Conversely, authority transitions constrain which pending support may still be consumed: when a leader steps down it answers every inflight logFuture and pending verifyFuture with ErrLeadershipLost, and a follower that truncates a conflicting suffix also rolls its latest configuration back to the committed one, so an uncommitted configuration cannot survive on a minority that lost the election.

feedback.answered: The pipelined AppendEntries path is now sourced. On the transport side, netPipeline sends the request first and then hands the future to inprogressCh, while a single decodeResponses goroutine takes futures from that channel in order, decodes one response per future on the same connection and publishes completed futures on doneCh (net_transport.go 817-905); the channel is sized maxInFlight-2 so at most maxInFlight requests are outstanding, and Close releases the connection and closes shutdownCh. On the protocol side, pipelineSend advances its local next-index optimistically by the number of entries sent as soon as the request is accepted by the pipeline (replication.go 512-530), and pipelineDecode consumes the pipeline consumer channel in order: a response with a newer term stops the leader's replication via handleStaleTerm, the first non-success response aborts the whole pipeline by returning (replication.go 534-565), and only successful responses call updateLastAppended, which is what records the peer's match index and moves the shared nextIndex. So request/response correlation for the pipeline is FIFO-by-construction and requires the transport to deliver responses in send order on one connection; the library's recovery from any pipeline error is to abandon pipelining and fall back to the synchronous path rather than to resynchronise inside the pipeline.

Outbound: getConn reuses a pooled connection for the target when one is available and otherwise dials through the StreamLayer with n.timeout, wrapping the connection in a buffered writer plus a msgpack encoder/decoder (net_transport.go 403-430); genericRPC sends the typed RPC and then calls decodeResponse, returning the connection to the pool only when the response decoded cleanly (496-506), so a connection whose response failed mid-stream is released rather than pooled; returnConn keeps at most maxPool connections per target and releases the rest (434-446); InstallSnapshot deliberately never reuses its connection (509-511). feedback.answered: Three previously open transport questions are answered by reading. First, a pooled connection is exclusive: getPooledConn takes connPoolLock, pops the last entry of the per-target slice, nils the slot and truncates the slice before returning (net_transport.go 366-378), so one connection cannot be handed to two callers concurrently, and returnConn only re-pools below maxPool (434-446). Second, the NetworkTransport's consumer channel is created unbuffered - `consumeCh: make(chan RPC)` in the constructor (211-231) - so each inbound connection's handler blocks on its dispatch send until the Raft main loop receives, which serialises inbound RPC handling and makes head-of-line blocking the normal condition that the heartbeat fast path exists to shortcut; the main loop reads exactly that channel (raft.go runFollower/runCandidate/leaderLoop via trans.Consumer). Third, the in-process transport used by the captured tests delivers by pushing an RPC with a one-buffered response channel onto the peer's consumer channel under a send timeout and then waits under a separate response timeout (inmem_transport.go 176-199, reached from every typed RPC method at 101-174), and the two failures are distinguished in the error text ('send timed out' versus 'command timed out'); a send timeout therefore means not delivered, while a command timeout can return an error to the caller even though the peer already accepted and may still process the request.
